hook.text: A box jellyfish can kill a human in under five minutes with venom from tentacles 3 meters long.

buildup.text: Venom is injected—by fangs, stingers, or spines. Poison is ingested—by eating or touching.

discovery.text: Snake venom evolved from saliva proteins. Subtle genetic changes turned digestion into weaponry.

twist.text: Venom is expensive to produce. Many venomous snakes use dry bites as warnings to save venom.

climax.text: Scientists now derive life-saving drugs from venoms—blood pressure meds from pit viper venom.

punchline.text: Deadly to prey. Life-saving for patients.

quiz.question: What is the difference between venom and poison?
options: Venom is injected; poison is ingested

details.summary: Venoms are actively injected via fangs, stingers, or spines, while poisons are passively delivered through ingestion or contact. Both are complex chemical cocktails that have evolved independently hundreds of times, targeting specific physiological systems in prey or predators.
details.whyItMatters: Venoms are goldmines for drug discovery. Compounds from cone snail venom treat chronic pain, vampire bat saliva informs stroke medication, and Gila monster venom derivatives manage diabetes, turning deadly chemistry into life-saving medicine.
takeaways: Venom is injected; poison is ingested or absorbed through contact
Venom components target specific receptors with extreme precision
Venom-derived drugs treat pain, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes

faq.question: What is the difference between venom and poison?
faq.answer: Venom requires a delivery mechanism like fangs or stingers to be injected into the victim. Poison is harmful when eaten, touched, or inhaled. A venomous snake bites you; a poisonous frog harms you if you touch or eat it.

faq.question: Why are venoms useful for medicine?
faq.answer: Venom components have been refined by millions of years of evolution to target specific molecules in the body with extreme precision. This specificity makes them ideal starting points for drugs that need to interact with particular receptors or enzymes.
